title: Who must correct tax errors — and when should they be criminally liable?
label: 15 October 2026 · Draft Finance Bill evidence
summary: The committee examined two related proposals in the Draft Finance Bill: a legal requirement for taxpayers to correct errors in self-assessment, and a new criminal offence for making 'reckless' untrue statements to HMRC. Both witnesses agreed the correction duty is a major change that could help revenue but risks hitting ordinary, unadvised taxpayers hard. They warned the 'reckless' offence should not criminalise careless mistakes, urged clearer rules, stronger safeguards (including a de minimis, help for vulnerable people, and limits to high-value/high-risk cases), and suggested HMRC focus on bad advisers and improve its guidance and disclosure tools.

chapters.title: Big change: a formal duty to correct
chapters.takeaway: Giving taxpayers a statutory duty to correct returns is a major shift that could increase voluntary fixes but will hit people who don’t use advisers.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: We are looking at two proposals in the Draft Finance Bill: a legal duty to correct tax return errors, and a new criminal offence for 'reckless' untrue statements. Antonia, how important is the duty to correct?

turns.speaker: Antonia Stokes
turns.text: It's a significant change. It clarifies an uncertain area, but it's heavy-handed for low-income, unadvised taxpayers. Many won't know the obligations or how to correct, yet risk higher penalties if HMRC deems their failure deliberate.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: Think of a successful self-employed plumber earning £70,000 who makes a small error of a few thousand pounds. Should HMRC be chasing that person through this new duty?

turns.speaker: Antonia Stokes
turns.text: That feels disproportionate. The measure aims at low-value, high-volume errors, but ordinary people need simple processes and clear guidance—or they'll be forced into paid advice or penalised unfairly.

turns.speaker: Adam Craggs
turns.text: If the duty becomes law, it will settle uncertainty, but it will likely prompt a surge of cautious disclosures from taxpayers and advisers. That helps those who can pay for help; most people can't, and many won't even realise they should correct.

chapters.title: Practical barriers for ordinary taxpayers
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses warned HMRC’s disclosure tools, guidance, and support must improve, and vulnerable people need specific protections.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: If someone realises there's an error later—say due to a legal change—would HMRC have to tell them what to correct, or must the taxpayer figure it out?

turns.speaker: Adam Craggs
turns.text: HMRC should explain the basis for a correction, but many taxpayers accept HMRC's view. The bigger issue is that most people don't read tribunal decisions; they won't spot errors themselves.

turns.speaker: Antonia Stokes
turns.text: HMRC's current digital disclosure facilities are hard to use without an adviser. There are no clear timeframes in the draft law for when someone 'becomes aware' of an error or how long they have to act.

turns.speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
turns.text: Are there existing supports for people who struggle?

turns.speaker: Antonia Stokes
turns.text: Yes: HMRC has an 'extra support team' for vulnerable people, and charities like TaxAid help. But the extra support team is part of HMRC, not independent, and it cannot handle every unrepresented taxpayer who will need help.

chapters.title: Costs, de minimis and HMRC’s priorities
chapters.takeaway: Both witnesses suggested a de minimis threshold and questioned whether HMRC should focus resources on small-value cases.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Should there be a de minimis below which the correction duty doesn't apply?

turns.speaker: Antonia Stokes
turns.text: Yes in principle. HMRC might resist because it targets low-value, high-volume errors, but a minimum threshold would prevent disproportionate action.

turns.speaker: Adam Craggs
turns.text: I agree: pursuing small amounts can cost HMRC more than the recovery. There should be a practical value test so resources focus on higher-value or higher-risk cases.

turns.speaker: Lord Leigh of Hurley
turns.text: Should HMRC use better technology—wealth checks or AI—to spot undeclared income instead of this correction duty?

turns.speaker: Antonia Stokes
turns.text: HMRC must not rely on vague data trawls to trigger customer correction notices; any notice should be based on reasonable, defined suspicion. A better target is bad agents who inflate claims—HMRC should tackle those advisers end-to-end.

chapters.title: The 'reckless' criminal offence: do we need it?
chapters.takeaway: Both witnesses questioned the need for a reckless offence for direct tax and warned it risks criminalising careless mistakes; they prefer limiting criminality to deliberate dishonesty.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Is a new criminal offence for reckless, untrue statements necessary, given HMRC’s existing civil and criminal powers?

turns.speaker: Adam Craggs
turns.text: No. The comparable power in indirect tax (like VAT) is rarely used. Criminalising recklessness risks ruining lives for mistakes that should be civil matters; it's better to reserve criminal law for proven dishonesty.

turns.speaker: Antonia Stokes
turns.text: We haven't seen a convincing case for it. The examples in HMRC's consultation look like careless, not reckless, behaviour. If introduced, the definition of 'reckless' must be tightly drawn.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: Is this driven by political pressure to close the tax gap? How reliable are tax-gap estimates?

turns.speaker: Adam Craggs
turns.text: The tax gap is an estimate and necessarily imprecise—especially for unreported cash activity—so I worry policy may be driven by headline figures rather than clear evidence of a gap that this law would close.

chapters.title: Safeguards and practical fixes
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses urged concrete safeguards: de minimis, clear time limits, exclusions for reasonable reliance on advice, senior approval for prosecutions, and an initial focus on high-value/high-risk cases.

turns.speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
turns.text: If the Government insists on a reckless offence, what safeguards are needed?

turns.speaker: Antonia Stokes
turns.text: Tight statutory definition of recklessness; exceptions for reasonable reliance on advice; explicit exclusions for behaviour already covered by civil penalties; senior or independent sign-off before criminal charges; and limit use to high-value, high-risk cases.

turns.speaker: Adam Craggs
turns.text: Agreed. Criminal prosecutions have massive personal impacts even when people are acquitted. A statutory definition of recklessness and clear thresholds are essential, plus CPS oversight remains crucial.

turns.speaker: Lord Leigh of Hurley
turns.text: Should HMRC first improve disclosure tools and target bad advisers rather than widen criminal law?

turns.speaker: Antonia Stokes
turns.text: Yes. Better, user-friendly disclosure facilities, clearer guidance, phone support for worried taxpayers, and action against harmful advisers would likely improve compliance without criminalisation creep.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you both. You gave consistent concerns: the duty to correct is a big shift; the reckless offence risks over-criminalising; and urgent improvements and safeguards are needed if any changes go ahead.
